progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-seven verses in four movements: a remembered victory (2 to 9), a present defeat (10 to 17), a protest of innocence (18 to 23), and a demand that God wake up (24 to 27). It is a communal lament, and an unusual one, because the speakers refuse to confess any sin. For a learner it is the cleanest drill in the book for one pattern: from verse 10 onward the verbs arrive in a wall of second person forms with the suffix -nu, us, attached. You rejected us, You shamed us, You sold us, You scattered us. Read the movements in order and watch the same grammar change sides.

stichs.en: For the leader. Of the sons of Korah.
A maskil.

verses.summary: The heading is not part of the prayer: a director's note, a guild of Temple singers, and a genre label. Maskil marks a psalm meant to teach something, not only to be sung.

stichs.en: O God, we have heard with our own ears, our fathers told us,
of the work You did in their days, in the days of old.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with hearing, not seeing. The whole case rests on testimony passed down a family line, which is exactly what the rest of the psalm will hold God to.

stichs.en: You with Your own hand dispossessed nations and planted them in;
You broke peoples and drove them out.

verses.summary: Four verbs, all second person, all past. The conquest is told as the work of a hand rather than an army, and the same hand that uproots also plants.

stichs.en: For not by their own sword did they take the land,
and their own arm did not save them,
but Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face,
because You favoured them.

verses.summary: The point of the history lesson: the ancestors won nothing themselves. Sword, arm and land are named only to be denied, so the argument can rest on the right hand and the face.

stichs.en: You are my King, O God;
command the deliverance of Jacob.

verses.summary: Present tense at last. Having established what God once did, the speaker asks for the same thing now, and calls it by the old family name, Jacob.

stichs.en: Through You we gore our foes;
in Your name we trample those who rise against us.

verses.summary: The verb is borrowed from cattle: to gore with the horns. The strength is borrowed too, and the grammar says so twice, through You and in Your name.

stichs.en: For I do not trust in my bow,
and my sword will not save me.

verses.summary: The denial of verse 4 repeated in the first person singular. What was said about the fathers is now said by the one praying about himself.

stichs.en: For You have saved us from our foes,
and You have shamed those who hate us.

verses.summary: The last verse of the good part. Everything to here is past tense and true, and from verse 10 the same grammar will be used against God.

stichs.en: In God we have boasted all day long,
and we will thank Your name forever. Selah.

verses.summary: Boasting and thanks, all day and forever. Selah closes the movement, and the very next word in the psalm reverses everything said so far.

stichs.en: Yet You have rejected us and put us to shame,
and You no longer go out with our armies.

verses.summary: One small word turns the psalm. From here to verse 17 every verb is second person with us attached to it: You rejected us, You shamed us, You sold us.

stichs.en: You make us fall back before the foe,
and those who hate us plunder us at will.

verses.summary: Retreat described as something done to the army rather than by it. The subject of the verb is God; the soldiers only move.

stichs.en: You hand us over like sheep to be eaten,
and You have scattered us among the nations.

verses.summary: Sheep for eating, then a people spread thin across the map. The two pictures do not match, and the jolt between them is the point.

stichs.en: You sell Your people for no money,
and made no profit on the price.

verses.summary: The sale is an insult before it is a loss. The charge is not that God sold the people but that God sold them cheap and gained nothing by it.

stichs.en: You make us a reproach to our neighbours,
mockery and derision to those around us.

verses.summary: The damage turns social. Neighbours first, then everyone in the circle: the audience widens with each word of the verse.

stichs.en: You make us a byword among the nations,
a shaking of the head among the peoples.

verses.summary: A byword is a people whose name has become an example of something. The shake of the head is the gesture that goes with saying it.

stichs.en: All day long my disgrace is in front of me,
and the shame of my face has covered me,

verses.summary: The we of the lament breaks into a single I for two verses. One face is made to carry the shame of the whole people.

stichs.en: at the voice of the taunter and the reviler,
in the face of the enemy and the avenger.

verses.summary: Two pairs of participles, four kinds of opponent, and not one of them is fought. What wounds in this verse is a voice.

stichs.en: All this came upon us, and we did not forget You,
and we were not false to Your covenant.

verses.summary: The turn to protest. The covenant is invoked as a contract with two parties, and the speakers declare their own side of it kept.

stichs.en: Our heart has not turned back,
nor have our steps swerved from Your path,

verses.summary: The word used of the army in verse 11 is used here of the heart, and denied. The body was pushed backward; the loyalty was not.

stichs.en: though You crushed us in a place of jackals,
and covered us over with deep darkness.

verses.summary: The concession inside the protest: yes, this happened, and it happened at Your hand. A place of jackals is a ruin where a town used to stand.

stichs.en: If we had forgotten the name of our God,
or spread out our palms to a foreign god,

verses.summary: The protest hardens into a formal oath, the kind that names the offence and leaves the penalty deliberately unspoken.

stichs.en: would God not search this out?
For He knows the secrets of the heart.

verses.summary: The oath is submitted for inspection. Since God reads what is hidden, the claim of innocence cannot be theatre, and that is the whole argument.

stichs.en: It is for Your sake that we are killed all day long,
reckoned as sheep for the slaughter.

verses.summary: The most quoted verse of the psalm, and the one that changes what the suffering means: not punishment, but service, and it happens daily.

stichs.en: Wake up. Why do You sleep, my Lord?
Rouse Yourself, do not reject us forever.

verses.summary: The boldest verse in the psalm. The verb is the ordinary one for waking a sleeper, addressed to God, and later tradition was uneasy about repeating it.

stichs.en: Why do You hide Your face,
and forget our affliction and our oppression?

verses.summary: Hiding the face is the standard biblical phrase for divine withdrawal. Here it is put as a question, which assumes there is an answer.

stichs.en: For our soul has sunk down to the dust,
our belly clings to the ground.

verses.summary: The body again, lower than in verse 16: soul in the dust, belly on the ground. The posture is prostration, and it is also defeat.

stichs.en: Arise, be our help,
and redeem us for the sake of Your steadfast love.

verses.summary: No vow of praise, no promise, no confession. The psalm ends on a demand with a single reason attached, and the reason is God's own commitment.

pardes.body: The psalm is built as a legal argument. Verses 2 to 9 establish the precedent: God took the land, the ancestors' swords did not, and the people have said so publicly ever since. Verse 10 opens with one word, {{10.0}}, yet, and everything reverses. The same second person verbs now describe rejection, retreat, a cheap sale, scattering and mockery. Verses 18 to 23 supply the piece an accusation of this kind requires, which is that the defeat is not deserved. Then the last four verses drop the argument for imperatives: wake, rouse, arise, redeem. Nothing is resolved. The psalm ends on the demand.

Two words carry the seam. {{11.1}}, backward, is what God makes the army do in verse 11; the same word returns in verse 19 as {{19.2}}, where the heart is said not to have gone that way, so body and loyalty are deliberately separated. The second is {{20.6}}, deep darkness, the compound Psalm 23 uses for the valley walked through in safety. Here it is what God spreads over the people, which reads as a quotation turned inside out. Note also the root for saving three times in the first movement: denied of their arm in verse 4, denied of the speaker's sword in verse 7, then affirmed of God in verse 8. And the verb in verse 6, {{6.2}}, is taken from an ox using its horns.

Verse 24 became a liturgical problem. The Mishnah (Sotah 9:10, with a parallel at Ma'aser Sheni 5:15) records that Yohanan the High Priest put an end to the Awakeners, and the Talmud (Sotah 48a) explains that these were the Levites who said {{24.0}} {{24.2}}, awake, why do You sleep, on the Temple platform each day. The objection preserved there is one line: does the Omnipresent sleep? A sentence a psalmist may shout in extremity was judged too much to fix as a daily rite. Verse 23 went the other way and became a text of martyrdom, read as the claim that a death suffered for the covenant is an act of service rather than a sentence, which is how the psalm's refusal to confess any sin is usually resolved.

The hiding of the face in verse 25, {{25.2}}, is read in the mystical literature not as absence but as a mode of presence: a concealment is still an act, and an act is still a relation. Sleep in verse 24 is read the same way, not as a lapse of attention but as a withdrawal of flow, a state that can be addressed and therefore ended, which is why the psalm can order it to stop. On this reading the refusal to confess is not defiance. If the concealment is not a response to sin, it belongs to the structure of the relationship itself, and asking why becomes the correct thing to say rather than an impertinence.
